Layer Normalization  
Jimmy Lei Ba  Jamie Ryan Kiros  Geoffrey E. Hinton  
University of Toronto  University of Toronto  University of Toronto  
jimmy@psi.toronto.edu  rkiros@cs.toronto.edu  hinton@cs.toronto.edu  
and Google Inc.  

**Abstract**  
Training state-of-the-art deep neural networks is computationally expensive. One way to reduce training time is to normalize the activities of neurons. A recently introduced technique—batch normalization—uses the distribution of the summed input to a neuron over a mini-batch of training cases to compute a mean and variance, which are then used to normalize the summed input to that neuron on each training case. This significantly reduces training time in feedforward neural networks. However, the effect of batch normalization is dependent on mini-batch size, and it is not straightforward to apply it to recurrent neural networks. In this paper, we transpose batch normalization into *layer normalization* by computing the mean and variance used for normalization from *all* the summed inputs to the neurons in a layer on a *single* training case. Like batch normalization, we also equip each neuron with its own adaptive bias and gain, applied after normalization but before the non-linearity. Unlike batch normalization, layer normalization performs *exactly the same computation* during both training and test time. It is also straightforward to apply to recurrent neural networks by computing the normalization statistics separately at each time step. Layer normalization is highly effective at stabilizing hidden-state dynamics in recurrent networks. Empirically, we show that layer normalization can substantially reduce training time compared with previously published techniques.  

**1 Introduction**  
Deep neural networks trained with some variant of stochastic gradient descent have been shown to substantially outperform previous approaches on various supervised learning tasks in computer vision [Krizhevsky et al., 2012] and speech processing [Hinton et al., 2012]. Yet state-of-the-art deep neural networks often require many days of training. Learning speed can be accelerated by computing gradients for different subsets of training cases across multiple machines—or by partitioning the neural network itself across many machines [Dean et al., 2012]—but such distributed approaches entail substantial communication overhead and complex software infrastructure. Moreover, they tend to yield rapidly diminishing returns as the degree of parallelism increases.
